title: 1.1 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can describe the ways we are all doers of math, and compare my math story with a classmate's — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: A Ferris wheel turns slowly against the evening sky. Each car is filling with riders as the line moves forward.
noticeStarters: I notice the number of cars is ___ .
I notice each car holds about ___ .
I notice the Ferris wheel cars ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder what math the operator ___ .
noticeAndWonder.imageAlt: Four scenes of people doing math in daily life: a basketball game, students in band, a park clean-up, and two people playing chess.

vocabulary.definition: Anyone who uses mathematical thinking — which is everyone, every day.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cualquiera que use el pensamiento matemático, es decir, todos, todos los días.
vocabulary.example: Splitting a bill, packing a bag, keeping score.
vocabulary.visual: Splitting a bill 4 ways at dinner — that is a doer of math.
vocabulary.cloze: Anyone who uses mathematical thinking is a ___ ___ ___.

examples.text: Working out you need to leave at 7:40 to catch the 7:55 bus
examples.why: You used numbers and reasoning to make a decision.

examples.text: Only people who finish a worksheet first
examples.why: Speed is not what makes someone a doer of math.

vocabulary.definition: Your own history with mathematics — what you have done, felt, and learned so far.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Tu propia historia con las matemáticas: lo que has hecho, sentido y aprendido.
vocabulary.example: “I liked math until fractions, and now I like it again.”
vocabulary.visual: “In 3rd grade I hated fractions; this year I can explain them.”
vocabulary.cloze: Your history with mathematics — what you have done and felt — is your ___ ___.

examples.text: “Math felt scary until I learned to draw the problem.”
examples.why: It describes how your thinking changed over time.

examples.text: “I got an 85 on the last test.”
examples.why: One score is a moment, not the story of your thinking.

vocabulary.definition: Something you already do well and can share with others.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Algo que ya haces bien y puedes compartir con otros.
vocabulary.visual: “I am good at mental math with money” — a strength you can teach.
vocabulary.cloze: Something you already do well and can share with others is a ___.

examples.text: Explaining your steps so a partner can follow them
examples.why: It is something you do well that helps the group.

examples.text: Something you are still learning to do
examples.why: That is a goal, not yet a strength.

vocabulary.definition: To break a number into parts that add, subtract, multiply, or divide back to it.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Separar un número en partes que se combinan para volver a formarlo.
vocabulary.visual: 78.5 = 70 + 8.5, and also 157 ÷ 2 — both rebuild the same number.
vocabulary.cloze: To break a number into parts that rebuild it exactly is to ___ it.

examples.why: The parts add back to exactly the original number.
The parts do not rebuild the number — 0.76 went missing.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, without counting every one.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una respuesta razonada, lo bastante cercana para ser útil, sin contar todo.
vocabulary.example: About how many people fit on the Ferris wheel?
vocabulary.visual: 20 cars × about 4 riders ≈ 80 people on the Ferris wheel.
vocabulary.cloze: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful is an ___.

examples.text: “About 80 riders” when the true count is 78
examples.why: Close enough to plan with, and it took no counting.

examples.text: Any number you say without thinking
examples.why: An estimate is reasoned, not random.

launch.narrative: This is your support small group for Lesson 1.1. We're going to slow this down and build it together, one step at a time. You can ask a question any time — that's what this group is for.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — We are all doers of math
conceptIntro.intro: Before any new mathematics, the book asks a different question: where does math already live in your day? We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Everyone uses math daily. We do it differently, and sharing how we do it makes all of us better at it.

iDo.title: Watch me estimate the Ferris wheel
lines: The Ferris wheel has 20 cars, and about 4 people fit in each car. About how many people can ride at one time?
I count the cars: 20. Then I estimate how many riders fit in one car: about 4.
I do not count every person — an estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful.

weDo.title: Let's decompose 78.5 together
lines: Every one of those is the same number wearing different clothes. Find two more.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "My first step is ___ , because the problem asks for ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: Everyone uses math daily. We do it differently, and sharing how we do it makes all of us better at it..

explore.instructions: Quick warm-up together: Every card belongs on the left. That is the point of this lesson — you are already doing far more math than you get credit for. After sorting, say which one surprised you.

diagram.title: Ferris Wheel Estimate: Cars to Riders
diagram.caption: Each group of 5 cars carries about 20 riders; four groups make 20 cars and about 80 riders, which is why 20 × 4 is a reasonable estimate.

connect.scenario: What we believe about ourselves, about others, and about what we are learning shapes us. Your classmate has a math story too, and it is not the same as yours.
connect.promptQuestion: What do you believe are your math strengths, and which area do you most want to grow this year?
connect.prompt: Name one math ___ you already have and one area you want to ___ . Then name one thing you learned from a ___ 's math story.

check.stem: The lesson says, “What we believe about ourselves, about others, and about what we are learning shapes us.” Why does the Strengths Inventory ask you to name a growth area, not only a strength?
choices: Naming what you want to grow shapes how you approach learning all year, just as naming a strength does
Growth areas are only for students who are behind in math
The growth area replaces the strength, since you can only claim one
Naming a growth area has nothing to do with your beliefs about yourself
check.explanation: A growth area is a belief about your future the same way a strength is a belief about your present — both shape learning, so the lesson asks for both, not one instead of the other.

check.stem: One student's math story says she liked math more once she started drawing problems; another's says he liked it more once he memorized steps. What is the point of hearing a classmate's story that is DIFFERENT from yours?
choices: It shows there is more than one valid way to be a doer of math, and you might borrow a new strategy
Whichever method is faster is the “right” one, so you should switch to it
If a classmate's story differs from yours, one of you must be doing math wrong
It doesn't matter — you only need to hear stories similar to your own
check.explanation: The lesson's summary says we all do math differently and learning about each other's strengths helps everyone grow — differences are the point, not a sign that someone is wrong.

check.stem: Which of these is the BEST example of a specific math strength for the Connect prompt?
choices: “I can explain my thinking out loud so others can follow my steps”
“I'm good at math”
“I got an A last year”
“Math is easy for me”
check.explanation: The check says a complete answer names a SPECIFIC strength, not a vague self-assessment like “I'm good at math” or “math is easy,” and not an unrelated fact like a grade.

connect.modelAnswer: One of my math strengths is explaining my thinking out loud, because I can usually say why an answer makes sense. I want to grow at not giving up when a problem takes more than one try. From my partner's story I learned that she liked math more when she got to draw the problem, which I had never tried.

diagram.title: Riders per Ferris Wheel Turn (6 Turns in One Hour)
diagram.caption: Six turns carry 78, 80, 76, 82, 74, and 78 riders — 468 riders in the hour, which is why about 78 riders a turn is a reasonable estimate.

approaching.stem: About how many people can ride the Ferris wheel at one time if it has 20 cars that each hold about 4 people?
choices: About 80
About 24
About 5
About 400
approaching.explanation: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4, which is about 80 people.
choiceFeedback: That adds 20 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: How many groups are there, and how big is each group?
20 groups of 4.
Multiply 20 × 4.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Aproximadamente cuántas personas pueden subir a la rueda de la fortuna a la vez si tiene 20 cabinas y cada una lleva unas 4 personas?
approaching.explanationEs: 20 carros con unos 4 pasajeros cada uno es 20 × 4, que son unas 80 personas.
choicesEs: Aproximadamente 80
Aproximadamente 24
Aproximadamente 5
Aproximadamente 400
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos grupos hay, y de qué tamaño es cada grupo?

approaching.stem: Which of these is a correct way to decompose 78.5?
approaching.explanation: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Decomposing means the parts must add back to the original number.
hints: Add each option and see what you get.
The parts must total 78.5 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Which total lands exactly on 78.5?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una manera correcta de descomponer 78.5?
approaching.explanationEs: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Descomponer significa que las partes deben sumar de nuevo el número original.
hintsEs: Suma cada opción y mira qué obtienes.
Suma las dos partes de cada opción. ¿Cuál total cae exactamente en 78.5?

approaching.explanation: 80 − 1.5 = 78.5. Decomposing can use subtraction, not only addition.
choiceFeedback: 80 + 1.5 = 81.5 — that moves the wrong direction.
hints: Start at 80. How far down is 78.5?
Check your subtraction against each choice: which one starts above 78.5 and takes away exactly that gap?
approaching.explanationEs: 80 − 1.5 = 78.5. Descomponer puede usar resta, no solo suma.
hintsEs: Empieza en 80. ¿Qué tanto hay que bajar hasta 78.5?
Revisa tu resta contra cada opción: ¿cuál empieza arriba de 78.5 y quita exactamente esa diferencia?

approaching.stem: Name one way you used math outside of school this week.
approaching.modelAnswer: I used math when I figured out I needed to leave by 7:40 to catch the bus at 7:55.
sentenceStems: It was math because I had to ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Nombra una manera en que usaste matemáticas fuera de la escuela esta semana.

approaching.stem: What does it mean to ESTIMATE how many people are on the Ferris wheel?
choices: Give a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful
Count every single person exactly
Guess any number at random
Refuse to answer without more data
approaching.explanation: An estimate is reasoned, not random, and it does not require counting every one.
choiceFeedback: Counting every person exactly is not estimating — that is an exact count.
A random guess uses no reasoning, so it is not an estimate.
Estimating is what you do precisely when you cannot count them all.
hints: Is an estimate exact?
Is an estimate random?
It sits between those two.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué significa ESTIMAR cuántas personas hay en la rueda de la fortuna?
approaching.explanationEs: Una estimación es razonada, no al azar, y no requiere contar cada uno.
choicesEs: Dar una respuesta razonada que sea lo bastante cercana para ser útil
Contar exactamente a cada persona
Adivinar cualquier número al azar
Negarse a responder sin más datos

approaching.stem: Tell one thing you already do well in math.
approaching.modelAnswer: I am good at checking my answer to see whether it makes sense.
sentenceStems: One thing I do well is ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Di una cosa que ya haces bien en matemáticas.

onLevel.stem: Tonight the Ferris wheel has 19 cars, and about 4 people fit in each car. Mia rounds 19 up to 20 and says, “About 80 people can ride at one time.” Is Mia's estimate reasonable?
onLevel.stemEs: Esta noche la rueda de la fortuna tiene 19 cabinas y en cada una caben unas 4 personas. Mía redondea 19 a 20 y dice: “Unas 80 personas pueden subir a la vez”. ¿Es razonable su estimación?
choices: Yes — 20 is close to 19, and 20 × 4 = 80 is close to the exact 76
No — she has to use 19, so 76 is the only answer allowed
No — rounding up always makes an estimate too big to be useful
Yes, but only because 80 is a round number
choicesEs: Sí — 20 está cerca de 19, y 20 × 4 = 80 está cerca del exacto 76
No — tiene que usar 19, así que 76 es la única respuesta permitida
No — redondear hacia arriba siempre hace que la estimación sea demasiado grande para servir
Sí, pero solo porque 80 es un número redondo
onLevel.explanation: 19 × 4 = 76 and 20 × 4 = 80. Mia's estimate is 4 riders high — close enough to plan with, which is what an estimate is for.
onLevel.explanationEs: 19 × 4 = 76 y 20 × 4 = 80. La estimación de Mía es 4 pasajeros más alta: lo bastante cerca para planear, que es para lo que sirve una estimación.
choiceFeedback: An estimate is allowed to change a number on purpose. Compare 80 with the exact 76 — how far off is it?
Check the size of the gap: 80 against 76. Rounding up moved the answer by 4 riders.
A round number is easier to say, but what makes it reasonable is how close it lands to 76.
choiceFeedbackEs: Una estimación puede cambiar un número a propósito. Compara 80 con el exacto 76: ¿qué tan lejos está?
Fíjate en el tamaño de la diferencia: 80 frente a 76. Redondear movió la respuesta 4 pasajeros.
Un número redondo es más fácil de decir, pero lo razonable es qué tan cerca queda de 76.
hints: Work out the exact answer first: 19 × 4.
Now compare it with Mia's 80. How many riders apart are they?
hintsEs: Ahora compárala con el 80 de Mía. ¿Cuántos pasajeros de diferencia hay?

onLevel.stem: You want to estimate 19 × 4 in your head. Which move makes the numbers friendlier without changing the answer much?
onLevel.stemEs: Quieres estimar 19 × 4 mentalmente. ¿Qué movimiento hace los números más fáciles sin cambiar mucho la respuesta?
choices: Round 19 to 20 — then 20 × 4 is a double of a double
Round 4 up to 10, because tens are the easiest to multiply
Add 19 + 4 first, then multiply the total by 2
Rewrite 19 as 19.0 so it looks like a decimal
choicesEs: Redondear 19 a 20 — así 20 × 4 es el doble de un doble
Redondear 4 a 10, porque las decenas son las más fáciles de multiplicar
Sumar 19 + 4 primero y luego multiplicar el total por 2
Escribir 19 como 19.0 para que parezca un decimal
onLevel.explanation: 20 is one step from 19, and 20 × 4 is easy: double 20 to 40, double again to 80. Moving 4 up to 10 would more than double the riders in every car.
onLevel.explanationEs: 20 está a un paso de 19, y 20 × 4 es fácil: el doble de 20 es 40, y el doble otra vez es 80. Subir el 4 a 10 más que duplicaría los pasajeros de cada cabina.
choiceFeedback: How many riders would that put in one car? Compare it with the 4 the problem gives.
Adding joins two different quantities — cars and riders. Which operation matches “4 in each of 19 cars”?
Writing 19.0 does not make the multiplication any easier — the numbers are the same.
choiceFeedbackEs: ¿Cuántos pasajeros pondría eso en una cabina? Compáralo con los 4 que da el problema.
Sumar junta dos cantidades distintas: cabinas y pasajeros. ¿Qué operación corresponde a “4 en cada una de 19 cabinas”?
Escribir 19.0 no hace la multiplicación más fácil: los números son los mismos.
hints: A friendly number is one you can multiply without writing anything down.
Which of the two numbers is already almost friendly — the 19 or the 4?
hintsEs: Un número amigable es uno que puedes multiplicar sin escribir nada.
¿Cuál de los dos números ya es casi amigable: el 19 o el 4?

onLevel.stem: Mia rounded 19 cars up to 20 before multiplying. Explain why that made the math easier — and say what she gave up by rounding.
onLevel.stemEs: Mía redondeó 19 cabinas a 20 antes de multiplicar. Explica por qué eso hizo la matemática más fácil, y di qué perdió al redondear.
onLevel.modelAnswer: Rounding 19 to 20 made it easier because 20 × 4 is a double of a double — 40, then 80 — and I can do that in my head. What she gave up is exactness: 80 is 4 riders more than the true 76. That trade is fine here, because she only needs a number close enough to be useful.
onLevel.modelAnswerEs: Redondear 19 a 20 lo hizo más fácil porque 20 × 4 es el doble de un doble — 40 y luego 80 — y eso lo puedo hacer mentalmente. Lo que perdió es la exactitud: 80 es 4 pasajeros más que el verdadero 76. Ese intercambio está bien aquí, porque solo necesita un número lo bastante cercano para servir.
sentenceStems: Rounding 19 to 20 made it easier because ___ .
Her estimate is ___ riders away from the exact answer.
That is a fair trade here because ___ .
sentenceStemsEs: Redondear 19 a 20 lo hizo más fácil porque ___ .
Su estimación queda a ___ pasajeros de la respuesta exacta.
Ese intercambio es justo aquí porque ___ .

onLevel.stem: A different wheel has 22 cars holding about 4 people each. Ana rounds 22 down to 20 and says “about 80.” Ben multiplies 22 × 4 and says “exactly 88.” Which statement describes both approaches fairly?
onLevel.stemEs: Otra rueda tiene 22 cabinas donde caben unas 4 personas en cada una. Ana redondea 22 a 20 y dice “unas 80”. Ben multiplica 22 × 4 y dice “exactamente 88”. ¿Qué afirmación describe con justicia las dos formas?
choices: Ana's is fast for a quick head count; Ben's is what the operator needs to sell tickets
Ana is wrong, because she changed a number that was given
Ben is wrong, because an estimate has to be a round number
Only one of them can be doing real math
choicesEs: La de Ana sirve para un conteo rápido; la de Ben es la que el operador necesita para vender boletos
Ana está equivocada, porque cambió un número que le dieron
Ben está equivocado, porque una estimación tiene que ser un número redondo
Solo una de las dos personas está haciendo matemática de verdad
onLevel.explanation: 22 × 4 = 88, and 20 × 4 = 80. Both are good mathematics doing different jobs: Ana's is quick and close, Ben's is exact. Choosing between them is a decision about what the number is for.
onLevel.explanationEs: 22 × 4 = 88 y 20 × 4 = 80. Ambas son buena matemática con trabajos distintos: la de Ana es rápida y cercana, la de Ben es exacta. Elegir entre ellas es decidir para qué sirve el número.
choiceFeedback: Estimating means changing a number on purpose. Is 80 close enough to 88 to be useful?
Ben was not estimating at all — he answered exactly. Is that allowed too?
Look at what each number would be used for before deciding either one is not math.
choiceFeedbackEs: Estimar significa cambiar un número a propósito. ¿Está 80 lo bastante cerca de 88 para servir?
Ben no estaba estimando: respondió exactamente. ¿Eso también se vale?
Mira para qué se usaría cada número antes de decidir que alguno no es matemática.
hints: Work out both numbers first: 20 × 4 and 22 × 4.
Now ask what each one is good for — a quick guess, or selling tickets?
hintsEs: Primero calcula los dos números: 20 × 4 y 22 × 4.
Ahora pregunta para qué sirve cada uno: ¿una idea rápida o vender boletos?

onLevel.stem: A third student looks at the same 22-car wheel and says, “About 200 people can ride at one time.” Why is that estimate not reasonable?
onLevel.stemEs: Otro estudiante mira la misma rueda de 22 cabinas y dice: “Unas 200 personas pueden subir a la vez”. ¿Por qué esa estimación no es razonable?
choices: It would mean about 9 people squeezed into every car, not about 4
It is wrong only because 200 is not a multiple of 4
It is fine — an estimate can be any number you like
It is wrong because 200 is too round to be an estimate
choicesEs: Significaría unas 9 personas apretadas en cada cabina, no unas 4
Está mal solo porque 200 no es múltiplo de 4
Está bien: una estimación puede ser cualquier número
Está mal porque 200 es demasiado redondo para ser una estimación
onLevel.explanation: 200 riders shared across 22 cars is about 9 per car (200 ÷ 22 ≈ 9), and the cars hold about 4. Checking an estimate against the quantity it came from is how you catch one that has drifted.
onLevel.explanationEs: 200 pasajeros repartidos en 22 cabinas son unos 9 por cabina (200 ÷ 22 ≈ 9), y en las cabinas caben unas 4. Comprobar una estimación contra la cantidad de la que salió es como se detecta una que se desvió.
choiceFeedback: Estimates rarely land on multiples. Try dividing 200 by the 22 cars instead.
An estimate still has to fit the situation. How many riders per car would 200 need?
Round numbers are fine in estimates. The problem is how many people that puts in one car.
choiceFeedbackEs: Las estimaciones rara vez caen en múltiplos. Mejor divide 200 entre las 22 cabinas.
Una estimación todavía tiene que caber en la situación. ¿Cuántos pasajeros por cabina necesitaría 200?
Los números redondos están bien en una estimación. El problema es cuántas personas pone en una cabina.
hints: If 200 people rode at once, how many would be in each of the 22 cars?
Divide 200 by 22. Compare that with the “about 4” the problem gives.
hintsEs: Si 200 personas subieran a la vez, ¿cuántas irían en cada una de las 22 cabinas?
Divide 200 entre 22. Compáralo con las “unas 4” que da el problema.

onLevel.stem: The same fair has a carousel with 31 horses. About 1 rider fits on each horse, and it runs 3 times an hour. Estimate about how many people ride the carousel in one hour. Use any strategy you like — then name the strategy you used.
onLevel.stemEs: La misma feria tiene un carrusel con 31 caballos. En cada caballo cabe aproximadamente 1 persona, y funciona 3 veces por hora. Estima cuántas personas se suben al carrusel en una hora. Usa la estrategia que quieras y luego di qué estrategia usaste.
onLevel.modelAnswer: I rounded 31 down to 30 because 30 is friendly. 30 riders each turn, 3 turns an hour, so 30 × 3 = about 90 people in an hour. The exact number is 93, so my estimate is 3 low. I used rounding to a friendly number.
onLevel.modelAnswerEs: Redondeé 31 a 30 porque 30 es un número amigable. 30 personas por vuelta, 3 vueltas por hora, así que 30 × 3 = unas 90 personas en una hora. El número exacto es 93, así que mi estimación queda 3 por debajo. Usé redondeo a un número amigable.
sentenceStems: My estimate is about ___ riders in one hour.
sentenceStemsEs: Mi estimación es de unas ___ personas por hora.

practice.commonMistake: Believing that 'doing math' only counts when it happens on paper in a classroom.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: Which statement best shows what this lesson means by “we are all doers of math”?
choices: Everyone uses mathematical thinking daily, in different ways, and sharing those ways helps us grow
Everyone gets the same score if they try hard enough
Everyone must solve problems the same way to be correct
Only the fastest students are really doing math
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes three claims: everyone does math, we do it differently, and sharing our strengths helps all of us.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has three parts: everyone, differently, sharing.
Which option keeps all three?

turnAndTalk.question: The Ferris wheel has 20 cars, and you estimated about 4 riders fit in each car. Why is 20 × 4 an estimate and not an exact count?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The book estimates about 80 riders by multiplying 20 cars by about 4 riders per car, without counting every person.

stems.es: Esto es una estimación porque ___, no un conteo exacto.

turnAndTalk.extend: If you later found out each car actually holds 5 riders, would your estimate of 80 still be useful? Justify your answer using the new total.
extendStems: With 5 riders per car, the new estimate would be ___, so my first estimate was ___.
The estimate is still useful because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted cards like 'splitting a pizza fairly' and 'choosing the shorter line' as doing math. What do all eight cards have in common that makes them math, even though none of them looks like a worksheet?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Every card on the board describes a real decision — like splitting a pizza or checking if $12 covers two snacks — that uses reasoning or comparison, even without a written equation.

stems.en: These are all math because each one involves ___.
stems.es: Todas estas son matemáticas porque cada una involucra ___.

stems.en: The card that surprised me most was ___ because ___.
stems.es: La tarjeta que más me sorprendió fue ___ porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Could you find an example from YOUR day this week that belongs on the 'This is doing math' side of the board? Defend why it counts.
extendStems: My example is ___, and it counts as math because ___.
It is like the pizza card because both involve ___.

turnAndTalk.question: The lesson says naming a growth area matters just as much as naming a strength. Why might sharing your growth area with a classmate actually help both of you this year?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The Strengths Inventory asks students to name one math strength AND one area to grow, plus one thing learned from a classmate's math story.

stems.en: My math strength is ___, and the area I want to grow is ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Is it possible for your growth area to become a strength by the end of the year? What would have to happen for that to be true?

turnAndTalk.question: One practice problem asked about how many people ride the Ferris wheel if it has 20 cars that each hold about 4 people. What strategy did you use to find about 80?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 20 cars of about 4 riders each is 20 × 4, which is about 80 people — a strategy of multiplying equal groups.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who added 20 + 4 instead of multiplying? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Adding instead of multiplying is a mistake because ___.

questions.stem: Which expression shows 4 groups of 5 students?
questions.explanation: Equal groups mean multiplication: 4 groups of 5 is 4 × 5 = 20.
40 split into groups of 10 makes 4 groups.
